speechtext: On Monday last when this .motion was before the house the Prime Minister requested that it be allowed to stand and intimated that it was his understanding that it was contrary to the practice of any government to produce in this chamber the names of those to whom rebates had been granted under the Customs Act. subtopic: REBATES UNEER CUSTOMS TARIFF
speechtext:
I do not wish to transgress the rules of the house by debating the motion, but I should like to make one observation in regard to this matter as it involves, if it is dropped, possibly the establishing of a precedent in the house which I think the house should be cognizant of before such action is taken. I quite understand the practice of refusing to disclose the business of any private firm in connection with its invoices .or docu-

Unemployment Relief Camps
ments submitted for the passing of goods through the customs houses or customs offices of the country. But this is something different from that. The point at issue here is simply this: that certain revenue having been collected and entering into the consolidated fund of the country, under certain practice and rules of the department, rebates are made under the statute. All that I am asking is that when a rebate is paid between certain times-all I am asking is when a rebate is paid out of the consolidated fund-the name and the documents authorizing such rebate should be laid on the table of the house. If it is now decided not to do1 that, I should like to intimate to the house that in my opinion it is rather an extraordinary ruling that the House of Commons is not entitled to information dealing with the important matter of the revenue of the country and the manner in which it may be handled in so far as rebates are concerned.

The matter was brought up in this chamber last week by the leader of the opposition, and I concur entirely in what he said. This wood-cutting is taking place on private property, and without the formation of a federal district or the assumption of some overriding control we have no right even to go on the property. That is my view of the situation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I was rather amazed to find the suggestion made that this parliament could deal with this matter. This parliament has the same jurisdiction over this matter as it has over the private property of any citizen of any province. The lands, mines, minerals and timber of the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec are under the control of the crown in the right of the province.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
And every other province.
M,r. BENNETT: Yes. The only properties we have are in the Northwest Territories, the national parks and our experimental farms. With respect to reforestation the position is the same. We discussed the matter with the provinces on one occasion, but this dominion

has no authority over these woodlands near this city and no control, direct or indirect, remote or near; neither can it touch them in any way, shape or form unless there were legislation specifically directed to that end, and then the question would arise of the conflict between the crown in the right of the dominion and in the right of the province, and the purposes for which the crown right of the dominion desires to exercise its powers of expropriation. The whole matter was considered in a case that went to the privy council in connection with the right of way for a railway in northern Ontario, and the supremacy of the crown in the right of the dominion to expropriate provincial crown land for that purpose under the Railway Act as against anyone else was upheld. But as far as this particular question is concerned, we can talk about it, but the only authority that can deal with it is the province of Quebec or the province of Ontario as the case may be, unless we amend our constitution, which the formation of a federal district would involve. For a federal district comprising parts of two provinces would of necessity require a change in the British North America Act itself, having regard to the provisions concerning our parliamentary representation.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I say to the right hon. Prime Minister that what I suggested as certainly within the competence of this parliament and government was a conference with the provinces concerned. I saw no reason why my right hon. friend might not call into conference with him the premiers of Ontario and Quebec, and direct their attention to the fact that the land immediately adjacent to the capital is being denuded of its forest wealth. My right hon. friend recalls that when Sir Robert Borden was Prime Minister he appointed a royal commission, which after considerable trouble and expense made recommendations as to the improvement of the capital of Canada and how the suggested improvements might be developed. Among the suggestions was the creation of a federal district which would take in a large section of the wooded country round about the capital. Up to the present time that recommendation has not been carried out. However, it is wholly probable that in the course of years some means will be found whereby there will be created a federal district which will have to do not merely with the beautification of the capital itself, but also of its immediate environs.
Unless some action is taken immediately, however, an amount of damage will be done

Public Works Program
to the whole area adjacent to Ottawa that will be irreparable. I do not know whether my right hon. friend has seen some of the areas that within the past year have been cut within a very few miles of the city. If not, and if he can possibly spare the time for the purpose, I understand that to-night at 7.30 there are to be shown in one of the rooms of this house some lantern pictures which disclose just what has taken place within the last few years. Hon. members who see those pictures will find that the only appropriate comparison for some of the areas that have been shorn of their woods are the devastated areas of the battlefields after the great war. Many acres of beautiful woodland adjacent to the rivers or to the highways have been ruthlessly destroyed. I say ruthlessly, because they have been cut for a mere pittance, the owners receiving very little, and some unemployed men who have done the cutting but a very small amount of pay. There is an obligation on the federal government to have regard not merely for Ottawa to-day as the capital city, but to the capital of Canada for years and for generations to come.
The serious part to-day is that most of the forests -of which I am speaking are on hillsides which have very little soil upon them. The soil that is there has been the result of the slow accumulation of centuries, and, once the wood is cut, a few rainfalls are sufficient to wash away practically all the soil. Therefore it is not a matter that could be repaired by reforestation. These hillsides will become bleak areas of rock and stumps.
With the dominion government paying out money for the purpose of reforestation under a reforestation policy, it seems to me that there is an obligation to retain what we already have, especially where it is certain that in the course -of time we shall have to -do something in -the way of reforestation, if it can be done then, in order to make good a very serious loss.
I expected to find my right hon. friend sympathetic with any movement that would help to preserve the beauty of this capital and its immediate environment. I think he has that at heart. I believe that all that is necessary at this moment is for him to call in, as I suggested, representatives of the two provinces. He is pretty busy himself; let his ministers call in the ministers who have to do with the highways and parks of the provinces, have a conference and see if they will not agree to d-o something on their part in the way o-f conserving this forest wealth, provided the dominion makes some contribution, such as the Department of the Interior
is in a position to make out of unemployment relief funds, in giving employment if you like to unemployed surveyors. At this time we are sending lads to the mining camps and prospecting; a million dollars or more was asked recently by the Minister of Mines for great surveys, and it was urged that a lot of university men out of employment would thus find some work. Surely a few of these men might be retained by the Department of the Interior to do this work.
If I may I would point out to the Prime Minister, so that he will appreciate how urgent this is, that the areas nearest the roads and the river banks and the lakes are cut first, because it is cheaper to transport the wood from them. I do not think there is any desire to prevent the men who own these little properties from making what they can out of cutting some of their wooded areas. I believe even a word of advice would cause many of them to reserve the forepart of their grounds and premises immediately adjacent to the highways and confine what cutting they may have to do to the interior of their property. At any rate a reforestation policy which would have regard to not cutting timber below a certain size would help meet the situation-.
I appeal to the Prime Minister not to let this matter just go by with the statement that we have not the authority or that we must amend the constitution. In the past no one has been stronger on conferences than the right hon. gentleman, and conferences with the provinces are always possible. However, some government has to take the lead and certainly the federal government owes it to Canada to see that the immediate environs of the capital are maintained-, if it is at all possible to do so, with at least some degree of their original beauty.

First may I

The answer to the question of why I let nine years go by, may I say,
Public Works Program

is that all that I am speaking of has taken place only within the last two or three years. I think I can explain the situation in a word. What is happening is this: It was not the owners of this property who conceived the idea of ruthlessly cutting down these forests; it was a few men who discovered that by taking contracts they could go to the different farmers and offer them small amounts for their wood, I think something like fifty cents a cord is what, in many cases, owners receive; and a dollar a cord is what these contractors have been paying for the cutting of the wood. Times being hard, they have found a number of people who were prepared to accept their proposals and sell and cut the wood at that figure, and as I have said owners have been selling wood in many cases at as low a figure as from forty cents to one dollar per cord depending on the quality of wood cut. The contractors make what little they can out of the sale of the wood through the extensive contracts they have entered into. It has been only within the last two years that what has been happening along the roadsides, the river banks and the lake shores has taken place, and it is for that reason that I am saying to my right hon. friend that I am sure another winter will work a dtegree of devastation that will be completely irreparable.
I hope my right hon. friend will believe that I sincerely regard him as entirely sympathetic to a movement of this kind, which aims at the preservation of these scenic woodland areas in the immediate vicinity of the capital. I simply asked for his cooperation in this matter because I believed he should and would be willing to give it.

speechtext:
I only desire to make
this observation:	One must face the realities
of this situation. My right hon. friend suggested that trees below a certain size should not be cut, and I can only say that at the present time there is a law in that respect in the province of Quebec. That is a matter over which the province has control so far as crown lands are concerned. We have no more control over those crown lands than we have over the island of Newfoundland, as the situation exists at the moment.
I do entirely agree with what the right hon. gentleman has said as to the dangers of this practice, because twenty-five years ago I bad occasion to learn of the evils of denuding a watershed of trees. Near the city of Calgary there was a fairly good growth of timber, which was under lease from the federal government to a well known company. A fire took part of it and the rest was cut down,

with the result that the humus which had accumulated during the centuries was washed down by the spring rains. Now there is no longer moisture gradually finding its way to the river; it comes down in the spring in the form of freshets, and there is no regularity of flow in the river. I discovered this in connection with an enterprise with which we were then interested, the use of water for the purpose of power. At that time we endeavoured to point out the evils of this practice. The company in question had a contract with the government which precluded them from cutting timber below a certain size, but the fire did the rest.
Every year, I think, this government has made some contribution for the purpose of preventing forest fires, and now that the dominion has parted with its interests in public lands, so far as the west is concerned, that part of the country stands in exactly the same position as the old provinces of Quebec and Ontario. The right hon. gentleman knows that better than I, because he had to deal with the agreements. We have no power with respect to the cutting of timber in the provinces of Quebec or Ontario and, what is even more important in this connection, we have no power in connection with reforestation. The province of Ontario had a reforestation plan, and after this depression began our director of forestry here was asked to look into the matter in connection with certain works that were carried on at one of the relief camps for single, homeless men in the Kananaskis valley, which is well known to the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart). The difficulty I see is that, with the best intentions in the world, this parliament cannot in any sense exercise control in this matter, since it lies with the crown in the right of the provinces to deal with questions of this kind. Eor instance, in the province of Quebec they have greatly improved conditions during the last few years by the reforestation of certain areas that have been denuded of trees. I understand that under modern methods they can carry on this work without very much expense, and I believe it has been demonstrated that it takes about sixty years for certain types of spruce to reach maturity for the purpose of being used for pulpwood.
So far as the immediate matter is concerned, I was not aware that the devastation to which attention has been directed was on such a colossal scale as has been suggested. However, I will ask the chairman of the federal district commission to communicate with the

Public Works Program
two governments concerned in order to ascertain from the ministers concerned in each of these provinces whether anything can be done to meet the situation. I am heartily in accord with the' principle that has been laid down, that the approaches to the capital city of Ottawa should be kept as beautiful as it is possible to maintain them, but I am also realist enough to know that unfortunately we have no power in the premises. If a federal district is to be set up, as I have pointed out, it cannot be done by this parliament alone; the district would extend into two provinces, and in the very nature of the action to be taken some modification of the existing provisions of the British North America Act would be involved. As I think the right hon. gentleman will remember if he carries his mind back, all these matters were discussed some time ago when the question of the federal district commission was being considered by the commission set up by the government of Sir Robert Borden shortly after he assumed office, which made a report on the beautification of this city, which to some extent has been carried out. As the years have gone by it has been found that the plans which have been carried out have resulted in this becoming a more beautiful city, and that work is being carried on all the time. If the approaches to the city are to be maintained, however, unfortunately it will require not only the expenditure of money; more than that it will require legislative action which is not competent to this parliament but which, in its ultimate analysis, will require some modification of the existing provisions of the British North America Act.
I shall direct the attention of the chairman of the federal district commission to the matter at once. I have no doubt he has had his attention directed to it already, because he and his commission have been most farsighted in trying to secure properties at reasonable prices in, order that the beautiful approaches to this community might be maintained. For instance, across the river an old mill burned down, and the commission were able to acquire that property at a very small price. Out near the research building two small properties were acquired for which we had to provide an amount in the estimates, in order to maintain just what has been suggested by the right hon. gentleman, the beauty of the community as a whole. But we will have to deal with the question of the approaches from an entirely different angle. I oannot do more than submit what has been said to the chairman of the commission, to whom I will send a copy of Hansard. However it may be desirable for him to go to Quebec and Toronto to see if anything can be done for the purpose of taking immediate action, for I had no idea that it was as serious as the right hon. gentleman has indicated.

I want to
protest against the expenditure of this money. I cannot understand why the government is constructing a highway from Lake Louise to Jasper before a trans-Canada highway is completed from coast to coast. Much relief work has been provided by highway construction but so far as I can understand very little progress has been made on the construction of the highway to the Canoe river from Golden. The Jasper-Banff highway leads eastward instead of westward and no provision is being made for a trans-Canada highway through Jasper to connect with the Golden coast outlet. To use the mildest language, it seems to me to be the height of folly to build a highway over a mountain peak 6,000 feet in the air and expect that the people from northern Alberta will be able to use such a highway more than one month in the year. An opportunity is offered of building an outlet to the coast at a height of little more than 3,000 feet which would be open practically as long as the roads are open in the province. The government has spent a considerable amount of money on the construction of this highway and yet no outlet to the coast is being provided. There will be great difficulty in keeping this road open, even in the summer time. Down at the southern end of the province a road was constructed around Crowsnest lake and it was found possible to keep it open only six months in the year. Finally a road had to be constructed at the lake level before it could be of any use at all. Yet the government is constructing a road up over 6,000 feet.
I am protesting against this money not being spent to provide a connection with the trans-Canada highway, in connection with which so many promises were made in 1930. Considerable money has been spent on certain sections of this highway but the construction of other sections remains in abeyance and no outlet to the coast is being provided for the people of northern Alberta.

Last year the hon. member took exception to the expenditure of money on the Lake Louise-Jaspei highway and advocated the completion of the west leg of the Big Bend highway and a connecting road from Jasper to Big Bend. Both
Public Works Program

these roads would lie outside the parks and it would naturally follow that the dominion would have no jurisdiction. The hon. member will recall that during his term of office correspondence was exchanged between this government represented by himself and the government of British Columbia in connection with the building of the western leg of the Big Bend highway from Revelstoke to the Canoe river. This year the dominion government will complete its part of the bargain by finishing the highway from Donald to the Canoe river. Owing to insufficient funds and possibly other reasons of which I am not aware the government of British Columbia have not fulfilled their part of the bargain. Certain work was done on the west leg of the Big Bend road during the past three years by camps under the jurisdiction of the Depart-of National Defence and certain boards of trade and other bodies have asked the dominion to take over the construction of that road. The fact that the dominion government is to-day constructing roads within our parks for scenic purposes does not prevent the undertaking of other road projects. The hon. member will recall that much money was expended upon scenic roads in the parks during his term of office and the building of this Lake Louise-Jasper road is simply a continuation of that policy. As far as the utilization of the road is concerned I have it on the authority of the chief engineer that the road will be available for traffic during the tourist season. A good deal of complaint has been made by the government about expenditures which they have been forced to make on relief. In Ontario, as my hon. friend well knows, and in the other

provinces as well, the federal government have been joining the provincial governments in the construction of what is known as the trans-Oanada highway. True, at the present time in northern Ontario there seems to be a disagreement between the two governments with respect to what they will do about the matter; but the well known policy of this government was to join the provincial governments, for relief purposes, in the construction of these highways; and my protest here is, first, that despite what the engineer or anyone else may say I know enough about the mountains to know that snow will not be out of passes six thousand feet in the air for more than one month. I know that from past experience because I had to construct a highway in southern Alberta where the summit is only five thousand feet, getting down to lake level at Crowsnest lake. Every engineer knows that, and any engineer who tells the government that a pass six thousand two hundred feet in the air will be open for more than one month in the year is straining his veracity to a great extent. What I am pointing out to the minister, as I pointed out last year, is that this government made very spacious promises in 1930 with respect to this trans-Canada highway. As a matter of fact, the electorate thought that the government were going to build this highway quite irrespective of any contribution by the provinces; and when the minister speaks of the cooperation we offered British Columbia with respect to the Golden-Revelstoke highway, let me point out that that was done for the purpose of avoiding an impossible route across Glacier park. We did it to avoid construction through the park at that point. There was no trans-Canada highway thought of at that time except for the general idea that we should get one across Canada, the provinces constructing every mile within provincial boundaries and we doing our part wherever it passed through crown lands, whether in the national parks or elsewhere. And with that in view the highway was projected to Jasper. We improved a good many years in advance of the arrival of the provincial government at the eastern boundary of Jasper park, the highway through the town itself to the boundary of the park, with the intention of extending that highway westward. At that time we had an agreement, or we were negotiating an agreement to take in Mount Robson park and add it to Jasper park, which would have entailed a good deal more mileage of highway within the park boundary. What I want to point out however is that the construction of the southern end over the summits, which they have adopted, is not going to provide a high-

way for any very lengthy period during the summer unless the snow ploughs are kept at work.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a question raised last week by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis) and the hon. member for Vanoouver North (Mr. Munn) in regard to the damages sustained by Stanley park due to unprecedented storms last January. This matter was, I believe, drawn to the attention of the Minister of Public Works last week by the two hon. members I have mentioned. I addressed some remarks to the Prime Minister just before he took ill and he promised to give the matter his earnest consideration. Since then it was also taken up with the Minister of Public Works and the correspondence directed to that minister was forwarded by him to the Minister of the Interior. I am sure the Minister of the Interior is conversant with the representations that have been received fnom the parks commissioner and other authorities of the city of Vancouver with respect to this work. An appeal was made to the city council and some assistance was received from them. A sum of $25,000 was received from the provincial government- and an appeal was directed to the Prime Minister for a grant of $50,000. I just wish to take this opportunity of reiterating what was said last week by my two colleagues from British Columbia and to emphasize to the minister the absolute urgency of this work, because this park is in every sense a national asset and its scenic beauty is unrivaled in the dominion. Tremendous havoc was occasioned by what was really an act of God, and I

appeal to the minister to make some grant towards the restoration and repair of that park in order to obviate a fire menace that undoubtedly exists at the present time.

speechtext:
This matter was drawn to my attention as well as to that of the Minister of Labour some weeks ago. After consultation, a joint recommendation was made to council and on May 10 an order in council was passed authorizing the Minister of Labour to enter into an agreement with British Columbia whereby a sum not exceeding $25,000 might be made available for -the purpose of clearing away the debris and putting into force silvicultural practice; further, a representative of the forestry branch of the Department of the Interior will be on -the ground and his services will be available to the commission or whatever body is chosen to prosecute the work, and moreover, that the value of the debris, which should amount to a considerable sum, 1 believe as much as $40,000, would also be expended for the purpose of clearing away the debris and doing as much repair work as possible.
Mr. STEiWART (Edmonton): May I just point out again to the minister what I stated with respect to the British Columbia agreement for the construction of the Golden-Revelstoke highway. I made no such statement as the minister indicated I did, but I pointed out to him that the federal government was spending large sums of money in conjunction with the provinces in order to complete this highway. I also pointed out that the general impression was, rightly or wrongly, that promises were made in the 1930 election that this highway was going to be a national undertaking from ocean to ocean and was going to be constructed as such. All of this has now apparently been abandoned by the federal government and the provinces are to do this work subject to whatever assistance the federal government is willing to give. As the British Columbia government have shown every evidence of being, to say the least of it, very dilatory in this construction, it seems to me that steps might be taken to render some assistance. I am not suggesting that it be done out of the vote under consideration. Might I point out to the minister that in my opinion this vote would have been better spent on the prosecution of the road from Jasper westward than on the construction of this scenic highway which he describes through the park. I am not objecting to the scenic highway, but it should be made secondary to the other. I want to register a very serious objection to

Public Works Program
making the summit some six thousand feet in the Rockies. That is a serious blunder and I do not mind saying so most emphatically. But that it should be commenced at all while the through highway remains in abeyance is something I do not understand and I wish to register a very strong protest in that regard. I hope I have made my position clear.
May I ask the minister this question:	In
Calgary they are leveling an air port. I brought this matter up the other day-I do not know what department it would come under.-and I thought I should have been here on Thursday night to receive an answer. New machinery at a cost of $35,000 was purchased by the contractor and put to work on that undertaking while literally hundreds of men are standing around unable to get employment. The answer I got from the Minister of Public Works was that in some cases it is cheaper to get the work done by machinery. What under heaven are we voting this money for, if not to give employment? If it is for the purpose of utilizing heavy machinery, then it is not relief work at all. I again wish to protest against what has been done in Calgary and to point out to the minister and indeed to all the ministers because every one of them seems to be interested in the expenditure of this appropriation, that it does not matter whether the work does cost a little more, for heaven's sake let human labour rather than machinery do the work and give employment to people who need it very badly. I want .to make that protest very strongly. I know I cannot lay the blame at the door of the Minister of the Interior because I have a pretty fair knowledge of how his work is being prosecuted and that all labour possible is employed. But when you find, as I discovered in Calgary, a situation of that kind, I want to protest most vigorously against that procedure being followed when work of this character is undertaken. Let those steam shovels and other machinery rust for a year or two and give men employment.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: In every case-, quite irrespective of cost, the work should be done by human labour. It is all nonsense for the minister to say to the house that a contract is let and the contractor purchases a new machine for $35,000 that can displace daily the labour of one hundred men. I do not deny the fact that machinery will do the work cheaper, but that is not what the parliament of Canada is voting this money for. This money is voted for unemployment relief. I protest in the strongest terms. No minister has yet come out and stated that as far as. this year's work is concerned it will be done-with pick and shovel rather than by machinery. We are anxious to have such a statement from the ministers. We had the same statement last year, and yet this year we find' work being done in that manner under the guise of unemployment relief, while three hundred men stand around asking for a job and none is to be had. The suggestion has been made to-day, and it was made last week, by some members of the official opposition that the government should do away with machinery. that they should let the machinery rot or rust and keep more people at work Lv giving them picks and shovels. In my *opinion to adopt such a suggestion would be simply to turn back the hands of the clock. 'To be logical why not go a little further; why not take away the picks and shovels and give the men trowels or even teaspoons? Then everyone would be kept busy. Surely we should approach this question in a different manner. In giving work we want to produce goods or those advantages for which the people are looking. If we have too many people idle to-day may I suggest that we could very soon get rid of a great many of them by reducing the age at which they would become eligible for old age pension, to sixty years. If that were done two hundred thousand people would be taken off the labour market. To-day we have no less than eighty thousand people over the age of seventy years who are still working. If full IMr. Marcil.J
advantage were taken of the old age pension, therefore, a very large number would be taken off the labour market.
Surely to-day we must realize that we should enslave the machine to mankind rather than turn it the other way around, as has been suggested, and enslave mankind to the machine. I strenuously object to turning the hands of the clock backward. I am in favour of using machines to the limit, so long as we see that the people have sufficient purchasing power with which to buy the things that are produced.

The minister said he had not the information with regard to the number which had been eliminated in rural sections, -but that he would get it. I should be very glad if he would, because it is a matter which is of great importance to the people in the constituency I represent. In passing may

Public Works Program
I state that I concur in the remarks of the hon. member for Prince. I do not know of any expenditure which could have been more advantageously made at the present time than one which would have had the effect of eliminating level crossings under a procedure which would have to be carried out by teams and hand labour. This work would give real employment, and I should be glad to learn the extent to which the crossings other than those in cities and towns have been eliminated by expenditures made in the last couple of years.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I shall look into the matter. Further, I shall be pleased to call the attention of the board of railway commissioners to the remarks of the hon. member for Prince because, as I have previously stated, the work of eliminating grade crossings is one which rests almost entirely in the hands of the board.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I should like to have that point cleared up, because I know the minister is always ready to give us all the information he can. I know however that it is no use to apply to the government to do away with level crossings; we must apply to the railway board.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Correct.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: It is entirely in their hands.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Yes, except in one regard
which, in connection with this vote, I should like to explain, so that there may be no misunderstanding. I stated the other evening that generally speaking the board of railway commissioners can give only a certain amount towards the elimination of grade crossings,- 40 per cent up to $100,000 were the figures I gave. I did say however that there might be occasions in connection with this vote where some municipality or railway might take the attitude that at the present time it could not afford to contribute its share, and I indicated that if in certain instances great dangers existed the government might, under this vote, contribute more than the 40 per cent to some of the smaller-and these would be rural- grade crossing eliminations.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Has the railway commission
absolute power to decide the proportions which shall be paid by the municipality and the railway company?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: There is no fixed proportion?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
No. For example, if the
road was built before the railway crossed it, then the greater responsibility would be on the railway company. If on the other hand the road were built subsequent to the building of the railway greater responsibility would be on the municipality which built the road. The dividing up or allocating of expenses in connection with the elimination of a crossing is a matter which rests entirely in the hands of the board of railway commissioners.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
There is a grade crossing
in the incorporated town of Borden which was brought to the attention of the board of railway commissioners. They looked over the situation and although the railway at that point is elevated high enough to permit the building of a tunnel yet we could not persuade the commissioners to take up their share of the work. I am very sorry to state that a very fine couple from the province of Ontario met their death at this crossing while touring in the province. The tracks are high enough to permit the building of a tunnel and in my view the board of railway commissioners are unreasonable in their stand. Of course it is not a very public crossing and yet as is indicated, it is dangerous. In addition, a section of the trans-Canada highway passes near that point. I sincerely trust that as the minister has promised we will get our share of the money.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: In view of the many thousands of level crossings throughout the country it would seem to me that the amount appropriated for their elimination is very very small. Has the board of railway commissioners ever made any representations to the government indicating that they feel a necessity for a greater appropriation to meet legitimate demands?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Yes, representations have
been made to the government by the board of railway commissioners suggesting increased amounts. As the hon. member knows, for some years the amount has been $200,000 annually, but under relief legislation in the past two or three years on two occasions the government has allocated an extra $500,000, a total of a million dollars, to the board of railway commissioners for this project. That is in addition to the regular allocation of $200,000 per annum. It has been suggested that we
Public Works Program

make a regular contribution, but no decision has been made. The million dollars in this bill, together with the previous million dollars and the regular amount of $200,000 in each year would give a total of $700,000 for each of the past four years. This money has been given by the government to the board of railway commissioners.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Is that as much as or more than the board of railway commissioners thinks is necessary?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I do not remember off
hand, but I do not believe they specified any particular amount. They did think however we should increase the $200,000. I doubt whether or not they suggested a fixed amount.
I	believe $700,000 per annum would be an amount which they would consider fair.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Under this vote does the government contemplate spending anything at the historic site of Fort Langley? Fort Langley was the landing place of Sir James Douglas, and is one historic site in British Columbia which should receive consideration.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
No expenditure for that
purpose .is provided under the measure.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Would the minister take under advisement the possibility of doing something at that point, because I believe it has been neglected. Does it come under his jurisdiction and is it recognized as a historic site?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I find that Fort Langley is now under the jurisdiction of this department, but that no provision has been made for an expenditure under the item now before us. However I shall be pleased to obtain an expression of opinion from the historic sites and monuments board, and this will enable a decision to be made.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Last Thursday the Minister of Public Works stated that under item
II	of the schedule, totalling $1,500,000, only $62,000 would be spent in the province of Manitoba. Would the minister verify that point?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: We propose to spend in the Riding Mountain national park the sum of $62,000 and $18,500 on Fort Prince of Wales.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: That is all that will be spent in Manitoba?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Out of this item of

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Does the minister propose to spend any money in the peace garden?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: The hon. member knows that this garden is located in a provincial forest reserve and is not under the jurisdiction of this government. In making up the tentative program for this $1,500,000, no amount was allocated to that area. This garden has a national interest as it was established to commemorate 100 years of peace between this country and the United States and to further the cause of future peace between the two countries.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Can the minister take any part of this $1,500,000 and spend it at random any place he chooses outside of the national parks or the territories?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: It is not the intention to spend this money at random. As I explained to the hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset) a few moments ago, it is intended to expend this money in the national parks and upon other projects which will be carried out in the territories.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Will the minister make it clear that his department will not spend any of this $1,500,000 except in public parks and upon dominion properties?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I endeavoured to make that clear when I replied to the hon. member for Rimouski. I understand that my colleague, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart) has made a similar statement. Last year a similar item was passed and the moneys were expended in our national parks, upon historic sites and lands under the control of the dominion.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
That is not very definite. With this $1,500,000 in his pocket the Minister of the Interior becomes a Minister of Public Works, in fact as far as money to be expended is concerned we have several departments of public works. I want to know if the ministers have the right to take any part of the moneys allotted to their departments and spread it around any place they choose in order to influence certain sections of the country? I think we should know just exactly where this money is going to be spent. I have received the same type of request as that received by the hon. member for Rimouski. Everyone seems to be under the impression that the different ministers can do just what they like with the money which has been voted to them. I think we should know what the situation is.
There is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, something I brought to the attention of the Minister of Public Works the other day. I

Public Works Program
have received information which I believe to be fairly authentic, although it is hard to prove, that on these public works a man must sign, seal and deliver a document that he has voted one way all his life and will continue to do so before he can obtain a job. This is a very hard thing to prove and if this condition exists in the department I hope the minister will see that it is remedied as soon as possible. I am not offering this by way of criticism of the minister as I have not been able to substantiate my information. If parliament is going to vote money to relieve unemployment I do not think party politics should enter into the matter in any shape or form. I told the Minister of Public Works the other day that in connection with the construction of a public building in Winnipeg less than one-third of the men employed had been on the unemployed lists. The Minister of Public Works indicated that that was a fairly large percentage and if that is so the government should do everything in its power to see that more unemployed are given work. I should like a definite statement from the minister that this $1,500,000 will be spent in the national parks and in other places belonging to the crown rather than at random.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I can give my hon. friend as definite an assurance as I am capable of giving that the money will not be spent at random. The tentative allocation of this money was given the other day by the Minister of Public Works and it is already on Hansard. With regard to the selection of men according to their political leanings, I may say definitely to my hon. friend that such is not the practice in the Department of the Interior and it will not be in the future. Perhaps he will forgive me for being a little jocular, but I believe it is very hard to obtain definite information as to the political leanings of anyone. My own personal experience has been that it is rather hard to find that out, and I think many other hon. members have found themselves in the same position.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Some of the officials in charge of this construction work may not be as broadminded as the minister and I am bringing this matter to his attention in order that he may look into conditions.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I think the best answer I can give to the hon. member is the statement that we have been conducting these national parks since 1930 without any charge of political patronage having been made against the department in connection with the choice .of labour.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: The minister will understand that we are on the eve of an election.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I should like to know how much of the amount voted in the bill of last year remains unspent and whether it will be spent this year.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: The unencumbered balance of the vote of $2,000,000 under the 1934 act is $979,234.43, which amount is available for expenditure during the current season. Whether it will all be spent will depend to a great extent on the progress that is made with various works, because it might be that some money would be unexpended this year, as was the case last year, on certain of the projects.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Perhaps the Minister
of Public Works could tell us how much of the total $40,000,000 voted last year was not spent last year.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The best estimate I can give is that about $2,000,000 had been spent up to the first of April.
Mr, VALLANCE: So that there is approximately $30,000,000 after the first of April. Then you have $3,000,000 and $17,940,000 that can be spent during this year. I want to say something in support of the remarks of my hon. friend from Rimouski. I think that when the public reads the title of this bill it may easily misconstrue it. This is an act to create employment by public works and undertakings throughout Canada and to authorize the guarantee of certain railway equipment securities. Reading that, one might readily come to the conclusion that even in this item which we are now discussing in connection with the Department of the Interior bridges could be included. In letters I have received the question is asked whether it will be possible for the government, without designating the place, to build a bridge out of this $1,500,000. I see my hon. friend from Rosetown here. He and I are both interested in a bridge which was provided for in the act of last year, the bridge at Outlook. A good deal has been spent there and is being spent at the present time but so far only in connection with the approaches; on the bridge itself not very much has been done. What condition is the bridge in now? I see it from time to time when crossing on the railway bridge and I should like to get a statement from the minister. When can we expect that it will be open for use?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
A contract for
the substructure has been awarded and the work is being proceeded with as rapidly as
Public Works Program

weather and the flow of the river will permit. The engineers are preparing specifications and we are about to invite tenders for the steel superstructure.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I want to discuss very
briefly a federal building which is now going up in Winnipeg. It evidently was in the understanding of the Minister of Public Works that the work should be done by hand labour without the assistance of large machinery, but I gathered as I glanced through the open gateway-that is about the only view one can get of it-that excavating machines were at work on the basement. If it was the belief of the Minister of the Interior and the Minister of Public Works that the work was to be done by men using shovels, which would have afforded emplosunent to very many more men than are probably working at the present time, and if the contractors on their own responsibility are substituting machinery for hand labour, I think we ought to know about it. Was this work supposed to be done by men using shovels, so as to afford employment to a large number of men? If so, it should be seen to that machinery is not permitted to be substituted for hand labour.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I was in Winnipeg recently and saw the work being carried on. The greater part of it is being done by hand labour.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: In connection with the Outlook bridge, do I understand that the minister said he was inviting tenders or that he was advertising for tenders?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: That has not yet been decided.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Is it the policy of the government to invite rather than to advertise?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: In the main the Public Works department have invited public tenders, but there are certain small works-

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: This is not small.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: -in connection with which tenders have not been invited publicly. I have dealt with that on several occasions. Each case must depend on its own merits. If it is not possible to secure fair, reasonable and proper competition by inviting tenders,, then public tenders are called for.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: The construction of the approaches has been done by day labour?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: The approaches were constructed by day labour but a contract was let for putting in the foundation.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Is the order in council of May 10 available regarding Stanley park?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I will see that the hon. gentleman obtains a copy.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: With regard to the $40,000 for salvage, walking out of the chamber I heard one hon. member from the opposite side remark, "That is good; $65,000 for Stanley park in one day. Twenty-five thousand would have been all right." I may tell the minister that the commercial value of all the timber in Stanley park would not be more than half $40,000 to-day. Will the minister give the name of the forest engineer or of the person who placed that estimate of $40,000 on the salvage ?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: The information was conveyed to me in the form of a memorandum or letter, not addressed to myself, but which I saw, from the chief forester of the province of British Columbia. If I remember rightly, and I have a fairly good memory, he estimated that there were ten thousand cords of wood which he valued at $4 a cord, which would amount to $40,000.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: It puts the parks board in a wrong light. It is not worth $4 a cord; you could not get more than half that. I have been in the woods all my life and in Stanley park, over every foot of it. A good many people think that it is virgin timber, but Stanley park was logged a good many years ago and the big trees are all gone. There are very few old timers. The commercial value of the timber there is not more than $20,000 to-day. It is only 600 acres. It is not fair to the parks board to say that they are salvaging $40,000 worth of timber. They might sell $40,000 worth of timber if they could cut it all off, but it would cost a good deal .of money.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I told the committee that I thought I could give some additional information in connection with the operations at Winnipeg. All the excavation is being done by hand labour. The only machine used is an air compressor to provide power for breaking rock.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Did I understand the
minister to say that the substructure of the bridge at Outlook had been let after public advertisement?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I did not say
that.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
It was let by invited
tender?

Public Works Program

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I want to ask the Minister of the Interior a question in regard to what was said by the hon. member for Bona-venture as to Indian roads. As I understand the matter, no part of this item is to be applied toward Indian reserves. Am I correct in that?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: But there is in the estimates an item for Indian Affairs providing this year for an increase of $340,000 over the amount voted last year. I wonder whether the minister could give us an idea how much money was expended on Indian reserve roads out of the amount voted then, because there is great complaint particularly from one of the reserves in my constituency with regard to the condition of one of the roads. I have had it mentioned to me by people who have attempted to drive over it that the road about which I wrote the minister and was unable to get a grant of, I think, $100, is at present in a practically impassable condition. Is there any fund from which that could be repaired, or is it the policy at the present time to leave roads on Indian reserves in that condition?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The estimates of the
Indian department have passed the house and I am sorry I have not before me the information as to the allocation of moneys which may be expended this year on different reserves. I could have given the hon. member the information when the estimates were before the house, but unfortunately I am not in a position to do so this afternoon although I shall be glad to give it to him by correspondence. I think the hon. member had reference to the moneys voted under the parliamentary estimates and not to the moneys voted under the Public Works Construction Act of last year.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Quite right.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member says
that that is quite correct. Again I can only express regret that I have not the information before me to tell him whether or not any money has been designated this year for work on the roads which he has in mind.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: My hon. friend will obtain the information, I understand?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I will be glad to see that the hon. member gets the information.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Could the minister tell
the committee what proportion of the money spent last year was spent on contracts that
were let by public advertisement, and what on contracts that were let on invited tender? Some of the contracts that have been let, for instance, for buildings, have been let without advertisement for tenders.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Is the hon. member inquiring about the vote of 1934 in the Department of the Interior?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Yes, I am inquiring particularly about moneys that were spent on buildings last year.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: There have been only two structures on which tenders have been invited; a list of contractors were invited to tender on those two. One was a bridge and the other was a public building.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Shingwauk home?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: The Shingwauk home was constructed by the Indian department, not the Interior. I understood the hon. member was inquiring about the vote in the Interior department.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: It was by invited tender?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: And the Qu'Appelle building was by invited tender?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Of the buildings erected out of the money provided under the Public Works Construction Act of last year, how many were erected after published advertisement?

subtopic: WORKS, 'UNDERTAKINGS AND GUARANTEE OP RAILWAY EQUIPMENT SECURITIES TO CREATE EMPLOYMENT

There is an amendment
of which I gave notice some time ago which I wish to move, to add the words "by public advertisement " after the word "tenders" in line 4. The section will then read:
Except as hereinafter provided, the minister or department of the government entrusted with the administration, management and execution of any of the works set forth in schedule A to this act, shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the construction and execution of such works, and contracts for all such -works and undertakings shall be awarded under the direction of the governor in council.
I do not think it necessary to explain the proposed amendment, because we discussed it before, and discussed it last year. Under section 7, in cases of pressing emergency where delay would be injurious to the public interest, or in which from the nature of the work it could be more beneficially executed under the control of the officers of the department, and where the engineers so certify, it can be done without public advertisement. There is no objection to that. That has been the practice for some time.

Public Works Program
But the great change which was made a year ago, and which I submit has worked badly is that tenders can be invited for practically any kind of structure up to any amount without public advertisement. This bill is to create employment by public works, it is really for unemployment relief. When the first unemployment relief act was passed after this government came into power it was explained by the Prime Minister, in reply to a question by Mr. Woodsworth as reported at page 66 of Hansard of September 10, 1930. The following is what was said:
Mr. Woodsworth: How is it proposed to allocate the amount between the various provinces?
Mr. Bennett: It is not intended to undertake that duty by this measure, but rather that the administration of the act shall be of such a non-political character that each particular claim will be dealt with on its merits without regard to any other consideration.
Now the very reverse of that has taken place. Take the two buildings built by the Department of the Interior and the Department of Indian Affairs, the new Shingwauk home, the lowest tender was $151,784, and for the Qu'Appelle residential school at Le Bret, Saskatchewan, the lowest tender was $164,926. Neither of these were let after public advertisement. According to the statement of the Minister of National Defence the only building which tenders were called after public advertisement by that department was the recreational building at the Royal Military College, Kingston. We have the barracks, block 2 at Calgary, $163,546 let without public advertisement, the mess building at Calgary, $147,250 let without public advertisement, the grading of the landing field referred to this afternoon, $128,756 let by contract with no public advertisement. We have the stable building at Calgary, costing $63,962 let without public advertisement.
The Minister of Marine stated that in practically every case contracts under his department were let without public advertisement.
The Minister of Public Works has let a great many contracts for regular public works after public advertisement; his iniquities have not been quite as great as those of the ministers in charge of some other departments. But he seems to think that the money voted under the Public Works Construction Act can be dealt with in a different way from that voted for regular public works, so he does not follow the system nearly as closely for those as he does for works done out of the regular
public works estimates. For instance he invites tenders without public advertisement for the substructure of the bridge at Outlook amounting to $134,522. He invites tenders not by public advertisement for the construction of the building at St. Joseph d'Alma, $24,100, also for the construction of the public building at Beauport, Quebec, $16,365 and for the public building at Berthierville, Quebec, $42,520 and for the alterations and additions to the building at Hull, $20,784. None of these contracts were let after public advertisement, while in a great many cases, as I pointed out the other day, he calls for tenders by public advertisement for buildings costing $3,000, $4,000, $5,000 and $6,000. I do not think there is any justification whatever for saying in regard to this particular bill, We just invite tenders, particularly when it comes to buildings costing over $50,000. And I have given cases of a number of buildings costing over $100,000. I do not intend to labour the matter. I just give these few instances to show the folly of expending public money in this way. Why is this done? Is it unemployment relief? It is not being carried out under the undertaking with regard to unemployment given by the Prime Minister, which I have just read and which appears at page 66 of Hansard for 1930. Is it intended to give an advantage to the friends of my hon. friends? I cannot speak with regard to a number of the buildings but I have made definite inquiry in some cases, and I am told that every contractor who was invited to tender was a Conservative.

I put that up to both Mr. 'Coleman and Mr. Hungerford, and I have before me messages which I should like to read to the committee as coming from both those gentlemen, who are the best authorities I know of on the railway situation. The one from Mr. Hungerford I received just a few days ago, because I wanted to reply to these railwaymen. I said: I do not intend to attempt to answer them myself, but I think you men should put in writing your opinions. As a matter of fact I did not speak to Mr. Hungerford at all; I had my deputy draw the matter to his attention. iMr. Hungerford's reply is in the form of a telegram addressed to me from Montreal under date of May 23, as follows:
Replying to your inquiry as to how the railways would be affected if the various car and locomotive building establishment were compelled to go out of business. It has never been the policy of this company to construct m its own shops any substantial amount of new equipment. While some of our shops are equipped and are suitable for the construction of a certain few classes of equipment, they are not suitable or equipped for the construction of the general run of new modern equipment. If car and locomotive building companies in Canada ceased to operate it would be necessary to remodel and further equip certain railway shop plants which would involve substantial capital expenditure and be a duplication of existing manufacturing facilities.
S. J. Hungerford.
The reply from Mr. Coleman is in the form of a letter addressed to me from Montreal. also under date of May 23, as follows:
The shops of the Canadian Pacific, with the partial exception of one shop, were not primarily designed, or equipped, for the work of building new equipment. To adapt them properly for the construction of a considerable amount of such equipment, at a reasonable cost, would involve capital expenditures for new machinery and' other facilities, which the railway company does not desire to undertake.
The policy of the railway companies in this country has been to operate their shops on repair and conversion -work and to refrain from entering into general competition with Canadian manufacturing companies so long as they can obtain material and equipment from
such companies at fair prices. No departure from that policy should be undertaken without grave consideration because of the disturbance to industry which would be involved.
We would view with concern the permanent closing down of equipment building plants in Canada, as in their absence, with return to normal traffic conditions, the demand for additional equipment would place the railways to some extent at the mercy of foreign manufacture.
Yours sincerely,
D. C. Coleman,
Vice-President.
That is the opinion of the two railway companies. I might deal with this a little more fully; it will probably answer the questions as I go along, because I have had the same arguments put up to me by every railway shop in Canada. speechtext:
Far be it from me to
appear to contradict the minister concerning the statement he made to the effect that the original proposal in regard to new equipment came from the private shops, but that statement I am sure is not quite correct. More than eighteen months ago I saw a memorandum prepared by officers of the Canadian National Railways calling for some 3,300 cars, among them 500 refrigerator cars, some general service cars, and two other types. So far as refrigerator service is concerned no type of railway traffic has increased as much in the last twenty years as has the refrigerator service. This increase is due to two factors, the increased movement of produce from the West Indies and from the Pacific coast, and the fresh fish trade both from the Atlantic and from the Pacific which has developed greatly during the last fifteen or twenty years. Much of the original refrigerator equipment is totally out of date; it is not fit for refrigerator work and is now used largely for the conveyance of potatoes and other agricultural products that have to be protected from the frost in the winter months.
There is no railway shop equipment to-day that can begin to compete with two or three of the private car-building plants in Canada. I say that with great deliberation, for I know the essential facts. Some twenty-two years ago we built the Eastern Car Company's plant in New Glasgow. The first order we executed was for 2,000 cars for the Grand Trunk Railway. Then came the war, and we undertook to supply 2,000 cars of the largest capacity ever produced in America, for the Russian government. These wr undertook to deliver on the tracks at Vladivostok. We fulfilled that contract, and within the specified date. Soon afterwards we undertook to supply 4,000 cars to the French government, and we put those cars over when great numbers of boats were being torpedoed, but we fulfilled our contract and so contributed very materially to the success of the allies in the war. When I say that no existing railway shops in Canada can compete with some of the shops I refer to, I know exactly what I am talking about. The Eastern Car Company have a plant at New Glasgow that cost $2,500,000. There is

Public Works Program
no similar car building equipment in Canada that will compare with it for turning out railway cars economically. That statement cannot be successfully contradicted. It may be in the interest of the railways to do a little repair work in their own shops from time to time to keep their organizations intact, but generally speaking the railway men of this country have been very well treated during the past four or five years. There are other .people in the country as deserving of being supplied with work as they are. That is all I have to say about the matter for the present.

For a few .minutes I wish to discuss some railway equipment and service that is required by agriculturists, particularly the stockmen. For a long time I think we have known but did not like to admit that the railways were losing traffic to the trucks. That has been increasingly true in the last few years. There are I think three reasons why the trucks are taking more live stock traffic from the railways each year. One is that the truck picks up the stock at the farm. Particularly if people live a long way from the station this service is appreciated. It is expensive for the farmers, yet that has not prevented them from using trucks, because this service means much to them, particularly now when it is hardly safe-in fact I think it is not now legal in Ontario-to drive live stock on the highways. It is very difficult for farmers who are at a distance from a station to get their live stock to the station except by truck. From my district, which is between ninety and one hundred and ten miles from Toronto, practically all the stock is trucked into Toronto, and one can see the duplication there must be of trucks going over the same highway on the same day. Another reason for the great loss of traffic by the railways is that they have, rather stubbornly I think, refused to partition the stock cars, and it has been left to the shipper or loader to do it at his own cost, while the trucks have been willing, to put in partitions, if necessary, at no extra cost to the shipper. A third reason why the trucks are gaining and the railways losing in the business of handling live stock is the cost of stops to complete the filling of a car which has been partly filled, while the trucks will make stop after stop without any additional cost at all.
In view of this situation the railways should do a bit of heart-searching. I have here a letter from the United Farmers Cooperative Company, Limited, which I wish to put on Hansard. It reviews this situation, blames the railway companies rather severely, and
expresses the view that before we vote money for additional equipment for the two railway companies there ought to be some reckoning from the point of view of shippers of live stock.
This letter is addressed to me under date of May 14:
We are giving you a report on the question of live stock handling by the railway companies for the last ten years, in which the United Farmers' Cooperative Company, Limited endeavoured to persuade the railway companies to instal permanent adjustable partitions in live stock cars, so that different types of live stock would be partitioned off, which up to the present time has been done by live stock shippers, drovers or owners as the case may be.
^ We had the cooperation of the Eastern Canada Live Stock Union, the Western Canada Live Stock Union, the commission houses on the different markets in Canada, together with members of each live stock exchange in Canada, also stockyard companies and abattoir companies.
Eventually the different concerns above mentioned formed what is known as the efficient handling of live stock committee, of which we are members.
We have held meetings regularly each year, and have been before the board of railway commissioners at Ottawa, before a number of freight' traffic commissioners and officials of both of the railway companies of various kinds.
Our committee got a number of models from different people interested in the question and exhibited these models before the board of railway commissioners and other railway officials; they were built and installed in one car of the Canadian National and' one in the Canadian Pacific were sent out to various, parts of the dominion for demonstration purposes and proved to be just what was wanted.
When it came to the point where the committee expected some action we were surprised to learn that the railway companies came back with the decision that they were not financially able to install the partitions in stock cars even after they were offered the patent right for Canada free of charge. These gates were hung on a steel track in the roof of the car and when not in use could be moved to the ends of the car and only occupied four inches at each end.
Then they go on to discuss the next point.
The railway companies did' build a few portable gates which had to be carried in and out of the car and which required two men to handle and was at best only a makeshift, but they wanted to charge the stock men $1.50 for the use of two gates per trip,-
They certainly wanted all they were worth.
-and still persist in charging $3 for a stop off for completion-
And they give an example.
-such as loading part car at Chatsworth-
That happens to be in my constituency.

[DOT]-and completing at Holland Centre, while truckers collect their load from various farmers with only the regular rate for the lot.
